claims.source: The effects of the expression of the mutant PHOX2B on wild-type PHOX2B protein and its transcriptional activity is not known in vivo yet, although in vitro data indicates that the mutated PHOX2B protein alters wild-type PHOX2B conformation and its ability to form homo- and hetero-dimers (Di Lascio et al., 2016; Trochet et al., 2005; Trochet et al., 2008), its affinity for DNA and coactivators, as well as its degradation rate (Nagashimada et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to in vitro studies.

claims.claim: Mutant PHOX2B causes the formation of cytoplasmic aggregates and fibrils in vitro.
claims.source: It has also been shown that mutant PHOX2B causes the formation of cytoplasmic aggregates (Bachetti et al., 2005; Trochet et al., 2005; Trochet et al., 2008) and fibrils in vitro (Pirone et al., 2019), and dysregulates the transcriptional function of wild-type PHOX2B (Di Lascio et al., 2013; Parodi et al., 2012), thus changing expression of important target genes such as DBH, PHOX2A and TLX2 (Bachetti et al., 2005; Di Lascio et al., 2013; Trochet et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Mutant PHOX2B dysregulates the transcriptional function of wild-type PHOX2B, thus changing expression of important target genes such as DBH, PHOX2A and TLX2.
claims.source: It has also been shown that mutant PHOX2B causes the formation of cytoplasmic aggregates (Bachetti et al., 2005; Trochet et al., 2005; Trochet et al., 2008) and fibrils in vitro (Pirone et al., 2019), and dysregulates the transcriptional function of wild-type PHOX2B (Di Lascio et al., 2013; Parodi et al., 2012), thus changing expression of important target genes such as DBH, PHOX2A and TLX2 (Bachetti et al., 2005; Di Lascio et al., 2013; Trochet et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: In addition to potential effect of mutated PHOX2B on development and cellular function in CCHS pathogenesis, the expression of wild-type PHOX2B has an important role in respiratory control that extends the developmental period and its reduction in CCHS may contribute to the respiratory impairment in this disorder.
claims.source: Our data suggest that, in addition to potential effect of mutated PHOX2B on development and cellular function in CCHS pathogenesis, the expression of wild-type PHOX2B has an important role in respiratory control that extends the developmental period and its reduction in CCHS may contribute to the respiratory impairment in this disorder.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings and their implications for CCHS.

claims.claim: The shRNAs used in this study were designed against the Phox2b mouse sequence which shares 100% homology with the Phox2b rat sequence.
claims.source: The shRNAs were designed against the Phox2b mouse sequence (Ref Seq NM_008888) which shares 100% homology with the Phox2b rat sequence (Ref Seq XM_008770167).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the design of the experimental tools.

claims.claim: Rats gained, on average, 160±4 g over the experimental paradigm.
claims.source: Rats gained, on average, 160±4 g over the experimental paradigm (naive: 158±19 g; NT-shRNA: 202±25 g; PHOX2B-shRNA: 133±7 g); we therefore applied an allometric correction to V̇E to account for non-linear effects of weight gain (VE ALLO) (Mortola et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the experimental animals.

claims.claim: The Gpr4 and Kcnk5 probes used are designed against the mouse mRNA sequence and show 94% and 96% identity, respectively, with rat sequences at the level of the target region.
claims.source: Gpr4 and Kcnk5 probes are design against the mouse mRNA sequence (Ref Seq NM_175668.4 and NM_021542.4, respectively). However, the alignment of the mouse mRNA sequences with those of rat (GPR4: Ref Seq NM_001025680.1; TASK2: Ref Seq NM_1039516.2) showed an identity of 94% and 96%, respectively, at the level of the target region (Base Pairs 1030–150) (BLAST program, National Library of Medicine, National Center for Biotechnology Information, NIH).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about the specificity of the probes used.

claims.claim: Loss of PHOX2B reduces expression of TH and dopamine beta hydroxylase enzymes in catecholaminergic neurons in vivo and in vitro.
claims.source: Since loss of PHOX2B reduces expression of TH and dopamine beta hydroxylase enzymes in catecholaminergic neurons in vivo and in vitro (Fan et al., 2011), it is possible that in NMB cells of the RTN, reduction of PHOX2B alters the transcriptional machinery of other proteins (in addition to GPR4 and TASK2) and impairs their function in central chemoreception.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Reduction of PHOX2B in NMB cells of the RTN may alter the transcriptional machinery of other proteins (in addition to GPR4 and TASK2) and impair their function in central chemoreception.
claims.source: Since loss of PHOX2B reduces expression of TH and dopamine beta hydroxylase enzymes in catecholaminergic neurons in vivo and in vitro (Fan et al., 2011), it is possible that in NMB cells of the RTN, reduction of PHOX2B alters the transcriptional machinery of other proteins (in addition to GPR4 and TASK2) and impairs their function in central chemoreception.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on known effects of PHOX2B in other cell types.

claims.claim: A reduction in Gpr4 and Task2 mRNA would translate in a reduction in the protein levels and consequent reduction of RTN neurons chemosensitive properties.
claims.source: Because no good antibodies are currently available to detect protein levels of either NMB, GPR4 or TASK2, our results are only based on changes in mRNA levels, thus we can only speculate that a reduction in Gpr4 and Task2 mRNA would translate in a reduction in the protein levels and consequent reduction of RTN neurons chemosensitive properties.
claims.evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation due to lack of protein-level data.

claims.claim: Loss of PHOX2B expression may have some effects on viability of RTN neurons in vivo.
claims.source: Although some cell death may be associated with either surgical procedures or off-target effects associated with the shRNA approach (McBride et al., 2008; van Gestel et al., 2014), it is intriguing to speculate that loss of PHOX2B expression may have some effects on viability of RTN neurons in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation.

claims.claim: Absence of PHOX2B is compatible with neuronal survival, at least in the experimental time frame of this study.
claims.source: Even though this is a possibility, especially with an even more severe knockdown, we did observe a large proportion of Nmb cells devoid of PHOX2B protein expression, suggesting that absence of PHOX2B is compatible with neuronal survival, at least in our experimental time frame.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of viable Nmb+/PHOX2B- cells.

claims.claim: The two pH sensors (GPR4 and TASK2) are expressed in the Nmb cells of the RTN in partially overlapping populations of chemosensory neurons.
claims.source: As previously reported, the two pH sensors are expressed in the Nmb cells of the RTN in partially overlapping populations of chemosensory neurons (Gestreau et al., 2010; Kumar et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Genetic deletion of either GPR4 or TASK2 impairs the central respiratory chemoreflex with maximal impairment when both sensors are eliminated.
claims.source: The expression of these sensors is partially overlapping in Nmb neurons of the RTN and the genetic deletion of either one impairs the central respiratory chemoreflex with maximal impairment when both sensors are eliminated (Gestreau et al., 2010; Guyenet et al., 2016; Kumar et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: CO2-chemoreflex impairment became significant (~30% VE Allo reduction vs. pre-surgical baseline) only when Nmb neurons of the RTN were reduced by ~63% compared to naive controls in previous lesion studies.
claims.source: In our previous study (and the ones of others), in which RTN chemosensory neurons were lesioned with Substance P saporin toxin, CO2-chemoreflex impairment became significant (~30% VE Allo reduction vs. pre-surgical baseline) only when Nmb neurons of the RTN (Nmb+/PHOX2B+ and Nmb+/PHOX2B- neurons) were reduced by ~63% compared to naive controls (medium lesion range: 50–81% loss of Nmb neurons; Janes et al., 2024; Souza et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research by the authors and others.

claims.claim: Even though loss of PHOX2B severely altered the chemosensitive function in a fraction of Nmb cells, significant changes in ventilation would not be expected with only a <50% RTN cell impairment or loss.
claims.source: Therefore, even though loss of PHOX2B severely altered the chemosensitive function in a fraction of Nmb cells, we would not expect significant changes in ventilation only with a<50% RTN cell impairment or loss.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on prior lesion studies and the current findings.

claims.claim: The lack of significant alterations in hypoxic response supports the lack of significant changes associated with possible loss of C1 function.
claims.source: To support the lack of significant alterations associated with the possible loss of C1 function was the lack of significant changes in the hypoxic response that has been shown to be dependent on C1 neurons (Malheiros-Lima et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that hypoxic response was unchanged and C1 neurons are known to be involved in hypoxic response.

claims.claim: The initial cell loss observed in both NT-shRNA and PHOX2B-shRNA groups may be attributed to some inherent cell death associated with the surgical procedure or with the potential off-target toxic effects associated with shRNA procedures.
claims.source: The initial cell loss, which we observed also in NT-shRNA, and more prominently with larger injection volume of virus, may be attributed to some inherent cell death associated with the surgical procedure (although not observed in similar studies performed by the same investigators, Janes et al., 2024) or, more likely, with the potential off-target toxic effects associated with shRNA procedures (McBride et al., 2008; van Gestel et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the cause of cell loss, supported by citations about off-target effects.

results.result: The manuscript provides extensive background on PHOX2B function in development, its role in CCHS pathogenesis, and the expression patterns of PHOX2B in respiratory-related neurons. These claims establish the scientific context and rationale for investigating PHOX2B function in adult RTN neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C34 and C78-C82 are well-supported by extensive citations to prior research. These background claims accurately represent established knowledge about PHOX2B's developmental role, CCHS genetics and pathophysiology, and the expression patterns of PHOX2B in respiratory control centers. The claims are appropriately attributed to prior work and provide necessary context for the current study.

results.result: The authors identify a knowledge gap regarding PHOX2B function in the adult respiratory network and conclude that PHOX2B is required to maintain proper CO2 chemoreflex responses in the adult brain, independent of its developmental role.
results.evaluation: Claim C6 accurately identifies the knowledge gap that motivates the study. Claim C83 is supported by the experimental data showing impaired CO2 chemoreflex following adult PHOX2B knockdown (C7-C9, C35, C57-C64), demonstrating that PHOX2B function extends beyond development into adulthood.

results.result: Initial experiments with 200 nl viral injection volume showed off-target effects causing cell death in both NT-shRNA and PHOX2B-shRNA groups, leading to impaired CO2 chemoreflex in both groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 are supported by experimental data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) showing similar cell loss and respiratory impairment in both control and experimental groups with high injection volumes. The authors appropriately concluded this represented off-target toxicity and adjusted their methodology, demonstrating good experimental rigor.

results.result: At 2 weeks post-viral injection with reduced volume (100 nl), PHOX2B knockdown resulted in modest reduction of PHOX2B+ neurons but no significant impairment in ventilation or CO2 chemoreflex despite some cell loss in both NT-shRNA and PHOX2B-shRNA groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C53 are well-supported by respiratory measurements (Figure 1) and histological data (Figure 2). The data show that breathing frequency changes were age/weight-related (C41-C42), modest tidal volume reduction at high CO2 (C43), but no significant HCVR impairment (C48). Histological analysis confirmed modest PHOX2B knockdown (~46% reduction in PHOX2B+ neurons, C51) was insufficient to impair ventilation (C53), consistent with prior lesion studies requiring >60% cell loss for functional impairment.

results.result: At 4 weeks post-viral injection, PHOX2B knockdown resulted in substantial reduction of PHOX2B+ neurons (67% reduction) and significant impairment of the CO2 chemoreflex, with reduced tidal volume and minute ventilation during hypercapnia but no effect on room air or hypoxic ventilation.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C64 are strongly supported by respiratory measurements (Figure 4) and histological data (Figure 3). The data demonstrate progressive PHOX2B knockdown (C57-C58) without additional cell death beyond 2 weeks (C55-C56), and specific impairment of hypercapnic ventilation (C60-C63) with preserved hypoxic response (C65). The temporal progression from 2 to 4 weeks (C64) and correlation with PHOX2B+ cell numbers (C69) provide strong evidence for a causal relationship.

results.result: PHOX2B knockdown did not affect hypoxic ventilatory response or adjacent C1 catecholaminergic neurons, indicating specificity of the effect to RTN chemosensory function.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 and C100 are supported by experimental data showing preserved hypoxic response (metabolic adjustments accounted for changes) and unchanged TH+/PHOX2B+ C1 neuron numbers (Figure 5B). This demonstrates the specificity of the PHOX2B knockdown to RTN neurons and the selective impairment of CO2 but not O2 chemoreception, strengthening the interpretation that effects are due to RTN-specific PHOX2B loss.

results.result: PHOX2B knockdown did not alter Nmb mRNA expression levels in RTN neurons, indicating that Nmb is not a transcriptional target of PHOX2B in adult RTN neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 and C10 are supported by mRNA fluorescence analysis showing no change in Nmb expression across groups (p=0.608). The use of NTS Nmb cells as an internal control strengthens this finding. This is an important negative result demonstrating that PHOX2B knockdown does not affect the RTN marker used for cell identification.

results.result: The number of PHOX2B-expressing cells in the RTN strongly correlates with CO2 chemoreflex response, with PHOX2B+ cells showing stronger correlation (r²=0.739) than PHOX2B- cells (r²=0.482), indicating PHOX2B expression is a good predictor of chemoreflex function.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 and C35 are supported by linear regression analysis (Figure 5E-F) showing significant correlations between cell numbers and HCVR. The stronger correlation with PHOX2B+ cells and opposite relationship with PHOX2B- cells provides compelling evidence that PHOX2B expression level is functionally important for chemoreception. The statistical analysis is appropriate and the interpretation is well-justified.

results.result: PHOX2B knockdown was associated with reduced mRNA expression of Gpr4 and Task2 (CO2/pH sensors) in Nmb+ RTN neurons, with ~34-39% reduction in average expression and ~64% reduction in PHOX2B- cells compared to PHOX2B+ cells, while the fraction of cells expressing these sensors remained unchanged.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C36, C72-C77 are well-supported by mRNA fluorescence analysis (Figure 6). The data show significant reductions in Gpr4 and Task2 mRNA levels in PHOX2B-shRNA rats (C74-C75) and specifically in PHOX2B- cells (C76-C77), while the percentage of cells expressing these sensors was unchanged (C73). This suggests PHOX2B regulates expression levels rather than cell fate. The methodology using CTCF measurements is appropriate, though the authors appropriately note the limitation of lacking protein-level confirmation.

results.result: The authors conclude that PHOX2B has a role in transcription of proton sensors in RTN neurons, that PHOX2B in the adult brain has an important role in CO2 chemoreception, and that reduced PHOX2B expression in CCHS may contribute to impaired central chemoreflex function beyond the developmental period.
results.evaluation: Claim C37 is an inference from the mRNA data (C74-C77) suggesting PHOX2B regulates Gpr4 and Task2 transcription. While the correlation is strong, the authors appropriately acknowledge they cannot confirm protein levels (C93) or rule out other transcriptional targets (C92). Claims C13-C14 and C87 extend these findings to CCHS pathogenesis, but this remains speculative as the study used wild-type PHOX2B knockdown in adult rats, not mutant PHOX2B in a developmental context. The conclusions are reasonable hypotheses but require additional validation including protein measurements, direct transcriptional assays, and studies in CCHS models.

results.result: The manuscript discusses potential mechanisms by which mutant PHOX2B affects cellular function and speculates about additional transcriptional targets beyond Gpr4 and Task2, effects on neuronal viability, and the relationship between mRNA and protein levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C86 and C91 are appropriately supported by citations to prior in vitro research. Claims C92-C95 are explicitly identified as speculation by the authors, acknowledging limitations in the current data. The authors appropriately distinguish between what is demonstrated (mRNA changes) and what remains uncertain (protein levels, additional targets, effects on viability). This represents good scientific practice in discussing limitations and future directions.

results.result: The manuscript provides methodological details about shRNA design, animal weight changes, probe specificity, and comparisons to prior lesion studies to contextualize the findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 provide important methodological validation showing 100% homology between mouse and rat Phox2b sequences (C88) and 94-96% identity for the Gpr4/Task2 probes (C90). Claims C98-C99 appropriately reference prior lesion studies to explain why modest knockdown at 2 weeks did not impair ventilation. Claim C101 discusses potential sources of cell loss. These methodological and contextual claims are well-supported and strengthen the interpretation of results.

results.result: PHOX2B knockdown in RTN neurons was achieved using a viral shRNA approach, with progressive reduction in PHOX2B expression over time. At 2 weeks post-injection, there was a modest reduction in Nmb+/PHOX2B+ neurons (46.2% vs naive) but no impairment in ventilation. By 4 weeks, Nmb+/PHOX2B+ cells were reduced by 67% compared to naive rats, with a corresponding increase in Nmb+/PHOX2B- cells, and the progressive knockdown was specific to PHOX2B-shRNA treatment without additional cell death beyond 2 weeks.
results.evaluation: All reviewers acknowledged the progressive and time-dependent knockdown of PHOX2B. Reviewer 1 noted 'the authors demonstrate that knockdown efficiency is time-dependent, with a progressive decrease in the number of Nmb-expressing RTN neurons that co-express PHOX2B over a four-week period.' Reviewer 2 similarly affirmed the approach and findings. The methodology and histological quantification were accepted as convincing evidence of successful PHOX2B knockdown.

results.result: At 2 weeks post-viral injection, PHOX2B knockdown did not significantly impair the hypercapnic ventilatory response (HCVR) despite modest PHOX2B reduction. Breathing frequency was reduced across all groups (likely due to age/weight gain), tidal volume showed minor reductions in PHOX2B-shRNA rats at high CO2, but overall ventilation and HCVR were not significantly different from controls.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings as part of the time-course analysis. Reviewer 1 noted that 'despite modest loss of Nmb+ neurons in NT-shRNA and a reduction in the proportion of Nmb neurons expressing PHOX2B in PHOX2B-shRNA rats, 2 weeks of PHOX2B shRNA viral infection was not sufficient to impair ventilation.' The lack of functional impairment at 2 weeks was not questioned and served to establish the progressive nature of the effect.

results.result: At 4 weeks post-viral injection, PHOX2B-shRNA rats showed significant impairment in ventilatory responses to hypercapnia. Tidal volume, allometric ventilation (VE ALLO), and the hypercapnic ventilatory response (HCVR) were all significantly reduced in PHOX2B-shRNA rats compared to baseline, naive, and NT-shRNA controls specifically during 7.2% CO2 exposure. The HCVR impairment developed progressively between weeks 2 and 4.
results.evaluation: All reviewers affirmed these findings as convincing. Reviewer 1 stated 'their results convincingly show hypoventilation, particularly in 7.2% CO2 only, for PHOX2B-shRNA RTN-injected rats after four weeks compared to naïve and non-PHOX2B-shRNA targeted (NT-shRNA) RTN-injected rats.' The editor's summary noted 'convincing results show blunted ventilation during elevated inhaled CO2 (hypercapnia) with knockdown of PHOX2B.' This is the core functional finding of the study.

results.result: PHOX2B knockdown did not affect the hypoxic ventilatory response or baseline breathing in room air. The lack of effect on hypoxia was attributed to metabolic adjustments occurring across all treatment groups.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the specificity of the CO2 response impairment. Reviewer 1 noted the results 'suggesting a specific impairment of chemosensitive properties in RTN neurons with PHOX2B knockdown' (i.e., specific to CO2, not hypoxia). Reviewer 3 acknowledged 'this corresponded with a diminished ventilatory response to CO2 but did not impact baseline breathing or the hypoxic ventilatory response,' treating this as an established finding.

results.result: There was a significant correlation between the number of Nmb+/PHOX2B+ cells (r²=0.739, p<0.001) and Nmb+/PHOX2B- cells (r²=0.482, p<0.001) with the HCVR, suggesting that the number of PHOX2B-expressing cells in the RTN is a good predictor of the chemoreflex response.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly affirmed this analysis: 'Analysis of the association between PHOX2B knockdown in RTN neurons and the attenuation of the hypercapnic ventilatory response (HCVR)... showed a significant correlation between HCVR and number of Nmb+/PHOX2B+ and Nmb+/PHOX2B- cells, suggesting that the number of PHOX2B-expressing cells in the RTN is a predictor of the chemoreflex response.' This correlation analysis was treated as a strength of the study.

results.result: PHOX2B knockdown did not alter Nmb mRNA expression levels but was associated with reduced expression of Gpr4 and Task2 mRNA in Nmb-expressing RTN neurons. The fraction of Nmb cells expressing these pH sensors remained unchanged, but the averaged fluorescence intensity (mRNA levels) for both Gpr4 and Task2 was significantly reduced (~34-39%) in PHOX2B-shRNA rats. Within PHOX2B-shRNA animals, Nmb+/PHOX2B- cells showed ~63% reduction in both Gpr4 and Task2 mRNA compared to Nmb+/PHOX2B+ cells.
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledged the mRNA data, they raised concerns about interpretation. Reviewer 1 noted as a weakness: 'The inferences about RTN neuronal expression of NMB, GPR4, or TASK2 are based on changes in mRNA levels, so it remains speculation that the observed reduction in Gpr4 and Task2 mRNA translates to a reduction in the protein levels and associated reduction of RTN neuronal chemosensitive properties.' Reviewer 3 raised a critical question: 'How do you get a loss of Nmb+ neurons (Figs 2-3) with no change in Nmb fluorescence (Fig. 5B)? In the absence of representative images these results are not compelling and should be substantiated by more readily quantifiable approaches like qPCR.' The mRNA findings are accepted as data but their interpretation and relationship to function remain uncertain.

results.result: The authors suggest that PHOX2B has a role in the transcription of proton sensors (GPR4 and TASK2) in RTN neurons, and that reduction in Gpr4 and Task2 mRNA would translate to reduced protein levels and consequent reduction of RTN neuronal chemosensitive properties.
results.evaluation: This mechanistic interpretation was explicitly questioned by reviewers. Reviewer 1 stated it 'remains speculation that the observed reduction in Gpr4 and Task2 mRNA translates to a reduction in the protein levels.' Reviewer 3 raised a fundamental concern: 'It's not clear whether PHOX2B is important for transcription of pH sensing machinery, cell health or both. If knockdown of PHOX2B knockdown results in loss of RTN neurons this is also expected to decrease Task2 and Gpr4 levels, albeit by a transcription-independent mechanism.' The causal link between PHOX2B and transcriptional regulation of pH sensors is not definitively established.

results.result: PHOX2B knockdown did not affect TH+ (tyrosine hydroxylase positive) cell numbers or TH+/PHOX2B+ neurons in the C1 region, suggesting the viral approach did not significantly impact nearby catecholaminergic neurons.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 raised concerns about targeting specificity, noting 'the C1 and facial partly overlap with the RTN at this level of the medulla' and questioned 'how this non-cell type specific viral approach was targeted to Nmb cells but not near by TH+ cells.' However, the data showing no change in TH+ cells was presented and not directly challenged. The authors' interpretation that C1 neurons were not significantly affected is supported by the lack of hypoxic response impairment, as noted in the manuscript and accepted by reviewers.

results.result: Initial experiments with higher viral injection volumes (200 nl) showed off-target effects causing cell death in both NT-shRNA and PHOX2B-shRNA groups. The authors concluded this was due to toxic effects of the shRNA viral constructs. Even with optimized lower volumes, some initial cell loss (~15% in NT-shRNA at 2 weeks) was observed, attributed to surgical procedures or off-target shRNA effects.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged this as a limitation but accepted the authors' interpretation and optimization. Reviewer 1 noted as a weakness: 'The authors found a significant decrease in the total number of Nmb+ RTN neurons... in NT-shRNA rats at two weeks post viral injection... suggesting some inherent cell death possibly due to off-target toxic effects associated with shRNA procedures.' This was treated as a methodological limitation that the authors addressed by reducing injection volumes, and the remaining analysis was conducted with the optimized protocol.

results.result: The authors conclude that PHOX2B in the adult brain has an important role in CO2 chemoreception, independent of its developmental role. They suggest that reduced PHOX2B expression in CCHS beyond the developmental period may contribute to impaired central chemoreflex function, and that wild-type PHOX2B expression has an important role in respiratory control extending beyond development.
results.evaluation: All reviewers affirmed this main conclusion. Reviewer 1 stated: 'This study's results show that independent of its role during development, PHOX2B is still required to maintain proper CO2 chemoreflex responses in the adult brain, and its reduction in CCHS may contribute to the respiratory impairment in this disorder.' Reviewer 2 noted: 'The findings of this research underscore that beyond its developmental role, PHOX2B remains essential for sustaining accurate CO2 chemoreflex reactions in the adult brain.' The editor's summary called this an 'important study' with implications for understanding PHOX2B function throughout the lifespan.

results.result: The authors speculate that reduced PHOX2B expression in CCHS may contribute to respiratory impairment, that PHOX2B reduction might alter transcription of other proteins beyond GPR4 and TASK2, and that loss of PHOX2B expression may affect RTN neuron viability in vivo.
results.evaluation: These are explicitly speculative claims acknowledged as such in the manuscript. Reviewer 1 noted the limitation that tissue sampling and mRNA-based inferences involve some speculation. Reviewer 3's concern about whether PHOX2B affects 'transcription of pH sensing machinery, cell health or both' directly addresses this uncertainty. While the speculation is reasonable given the data, reviewers did not treat these interpretations as definitively established.

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support the core functional finding that 4-week PHOX2B knockdown impairs hypercapnic ventilation (C59-C64). OpenEval emphasizes the temporal progression and correlation with cell numbers, while peer reviewers describe this as 'convincing' evidence of blunted CO2 response. This represents the study's primary result with full agreement.

Both support the correlation analysis (C69-C71) showing PHOX2B+ cell numbers predict HCVR. OpenEval describes the statistical analysis as appropriate and well-justified, while Reviewer 1 explicitly affirmed this as a strength showing 'PHOX2B-expressing cells in the RTN is a predictor of the chemoreflex response.'

Both support the 2-week time point findings (C41-C48) showing modest knockdown without functional impairment. OpenEval notes this is consistent with prior lesion studies requiring >60% cell loss, while peer reviewers accepted this as establishing the progressive nature of the effect without questioning the findings.

Both address PHOX2B knockdown progression (C49-C53, C54-C58). OpenEval supports the modest 2-week knockdown (~46% reduction) as insufficient for impairment, while peer reviewers acknowledged the progressive time-dependent knockdown. Overlapping claims show agreement on the temporal dynamics of knockdown efficiency.

Both address the progressive PHOX2B knockdown (C54-C58). OpenEval emphasizes the temporal progression without additional cell death beyond 2 weeks and correlation with functional impairment. Peer reviewers affirmed the time-dependent knockdown with 'convincing evidence of successful PHOX2B knockdown' through histological quantification.

Both support the specificity of CO2 response impairment with preserved hypoxic response (C65). OpenEval notes this demonstrates RTN-specific effects, while peer reviewers accepted this as evidence of 'specific impairment of chemosensitive properties' without questioning the selectivity for CO2 over hypoxia.

Both address mRNA findings (C10-C11, C36, C72-C77) but with different confidence levels. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with appropriate acknowledgment of protein-level limitations. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 1 noting mRNA changes 'remain speculation' regarding protein levels, and Reviewer 3 questioning the Nmb fluorescence results and calling for qPCR validation.

Both address Nmb expression (C10, C67-C68). OpenEval supports the finding of no change in Nmb expression as an important negative control. Peer reviewers questioned this in UNCERTAIN evaluation, with Reviewer 3 asking 'How do you get a loss of Nmb+ neurons with no change in Nmb fluorescence?' indicating concern about methodological consistency.

Both address the mechanistic interpretation (C37) that PHOX2B regulates Gpr4/Task2 transcription. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, acknowledging the inference requires validation including protein measurements and direct transcriptional assays. Peer reviewers also rate as UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 3 questioning whether effects are transcriptional or due to cell health, and Reviewer 1 noting protein-level speculation.

Both support the off-target toxicity findings (C38-C40) and methodological optimization. OpenEval describes this as demonstrating 'good experimental rigor' in adjusting methodology. Peer reviewers acknowledged this as a limitation but accepted the authors' optimization, treating it as a methodological issue that was appropriately addressed.

Both support the main conclusion (C83) that PHOX2B function extends beyond development into adulthood. OpenEval bases this on the adult knockdown data showing impaired CO2 chemoreflex. Peer reviewers affirmed this as the study's primary contribution, with all reviewers and the editor describing it as an 'important' finding with implications for understanding PHOX2B throughout the lifespan.

Both address implications for CCHS pathogenesis (C13, C87). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting the study used wild-type knockdown in adults rather than mutant PHOX2B in development, making CCHS extrapolation speculative. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED for the general conclusion about adult PHOX2B function but acknowledge limitations in direct CCHS application.

Both address speculative mechanistic claims (C14, C92, C94). OpenEval rates the overall inference as UNCERTAIN while noting authors appropriately acknowledge limitations. Peer reviewers also rate as UNCERTAIN, with concerns about whether PHOX2B affects transcription versus cell health, treating these interpretations as reasonable but not definitively established.

Both address the limitation regarding protein-level confirmation (C93). OpenEval supports the authors' acknowledgment of this limitation as good scientific practice. Peer reviewers raised this as a critical concern in their UNCERTAIN evaluation, with Reviewer 1 explicitly noting the speculation about mRNA-to-protein translation.

Both address explicitly speculative claims (C92, C94) about additional transcriptional targets and mechanisms. OpenEval supports the authors' transparent acknowledgment of speculation and limitations. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, noting these remain unresolved questions about transcription versus cell health effects.

Both address C1 neuron specificity (C66, C100). OpenEval supports the finding that TH+/PHOX2B+ C1 neurons were unchanged, demonstrating RTN specificity.
